content: Dry eye disease (DED) is a condition caused by various factors that result in instability of the tear film, damage to the ocular surface, and changes in neurosensory function. Patients with DED often experience symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, pain, and visual disturbances. Topical corticosteroids, known for their anti-inflammatory properties, have been widely used as a short-term treatment option for DED. However, their long-term use is associated with risks such as ocular hypertension, cataract formation, and infections. As a result, most clinical trials evaluating the efficacy and safety of topical corticosteroids have been conducted over short durations, typically lasting three to eight weeks. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of topical corticosteroids compared to no treatment, placebo, other steroidal or non-steroidal therapies, or combination therapies for DED. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, with the last search performed on August 20, 2021. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving topical corticosteroids, either alone or in combination with tobramycin, were included in the analysis. Comparisons were made against no treatment, artificial tears (AT), vehicles, AT plus tobramycin, or cyclosporine A (CsA). A total of 22 RCTs were identified, involving 4169 participants with DED. These trials were conducted in the USA, Italy, Spain, China, South Korea, and India. Most trials recruited adults aged 18 years or older, with one exception that included children and adolescents aged 3 to 14 years. The majority of participants were female, with a median of 79% across trials. The treatment duration for topical corticosteroids ranged from one week to three months, while the overall trial durations varied from one week to six months. Eight trials were exclusively sponsored by industry, and four were co-sponsored by industry and institutional or governmental funds. The risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2 tool, revealing that nearly half of the trials had a high risk of bias due to selective outcome reporting. Among the 22 trials, 16 evaluated the effects of topical corticosteroids, either alone or in combination with tobramycin, compared to lubricants (artificial tears or vehicles), AT plus tobramycin, or no treatment. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that corticosteroids likely provide a small to moderate improvement in patient-reported symptoms, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.29 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.42). They also likely reduce corneal staining scores by 0.4 SMDs (95% CI 0.18 to 0.62). However, corticosteroids may only slightly increase tear film break-up time (TBUT) by a mean difference (MD) of 0.70 seconds (95% CI 0.06 to 1.34; low-certainty evidence) and have little to no effect on tear osmolarity (MD 1.60 mOsm/kg, 95% CI −10.47 to 13.67; very low-certainty evidence). Six trials compared topical corticosteroids, either alone or in combination with CsA, to CsA alone. Low-certainty evidence indicates that corticosteroids may provide a small to moderate improvement in symptoms (SMD −0.33, 95% CI −0.51 to −0.15) but have little to no effect on corneal staining scores (SMD 0.05, 95% CI −0.25 to 0.35). The effects of corticosteroids compared to CsA alone on TBUT (MD 0.37 seconds, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.87) and tear osmolarity (MD 5.80 mOsm/kg, 95% CI −0.94 to 12.54) remain uncertain due to low or very low-certainty evidence. None of the included trials reported on quality-of-life outcomes. The evidence regarding adverse ocular effects of topical corticosteroids is highly uncertain. Corticosteroids may increase the risk of intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation compared to lubricants, with a risk ratio (RR) of 5.96 (95% CI 1.30 to 27.38). However, when compared to CsA, corticosteroids alone or in combination with CsA may either increase or decrease the risk of IOP elevation (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.25 to 8.33). The risk of cataract formation associated with corticosteroids is also uncertain, with a RR of 0.34 (95% CI 0.01 to 8.22) when compared to lubricants. This uncertainty is likely due to the short duration of the studies, which were insufficient to observe long-term adverse effects. In conclusion, the evidence for the outcomes of this review ranges from moderate to very low certainty, primarily due to the high risk of bias from selective reporting. For patients with DED requiring anti-inflammatory treatment, topical corticosteroids likely provide small to moderate symptom relief compared to lubricants and may offer similar benefits compared to CsA. However, the evidence is less certain regarding their effects on improving tear film quality or quantity. Additionally, the available evidence is highly uncertain regarding the potential adverse effects of corticosteroids, such as IOP elevation or cataract formation. Future research should aim to provide high-certainty evidence to guide clinicians and patients in optimizing the use of topical corticosteroids, including considerations of formulation, dosage, treatment duration, and long-term safety.
